title: Sartorius v. Siouxlands Presbytery
synopsis: Did a presbytery fail in its duty to condemn erroneous opinions by acquitting a minister on theological-error charges? The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the acquittal undisturbed. A complaint against a not-guilty verdict cannot provoke a retrial at the superior court; under BCO 43 the superior court may only annul or remand, not reverse, and the complainant bore the burden to show error from the record. The record contained the defendant's testimony, including recantations or clarifications, Defense Exhibit 1, and witness testimony sufficient to refrain from contradicting the trial court. The SJC expressly did not decide the defendant's actual views. A separate concurrence elaborated deference standards but did not change the judgment.

title: Crouse v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
synopsis: A serving deacon nominated for ruling elder complained that his session removed his nomination before BCO 24-1 instruction or examination. The SJC held the session erred by adding an unwritten pre-examination 'vetting' removal and that Northwest Georgia Presbytery erred in approving it: BCO 24-1's sequence—instruction and examination before the session determines eligibility—is mandatory. The ruling reserved the session's sound discretion and the treatment of frivolous or clearly disqualified nominees. The complaint was sustained and remanded for adjudication consistent with the decision.

title: Evans and Pitts et al. v. Arizona Presbytery

synopsis: The SJC declared Benyola's complaint against Central Florida Presbytery administratively out of order and incapable of being put in order, because Benyola was no longer a member of any PCA congregation and thus lacked standing. title: Harrell et al. v. Covenant Presbytery

Challenges to witness-judges, venue, and refusal to refer were rejected.

title: Robert M. Shive v. Central Carolina Presbytery

title: Steven Hahn v. Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery
synopsis: Hahn challenged Presbytery’s ruling that CTKPC Session lawfully excluded him from that congregation’s worship until a psychiatric evaluation addressed safety concerns. The SJC denied the complaint. Applying BCO 39-3.3, it found no clear error in the lower courts’ credibility and discretionary judgments, given Session’s familiarity with the people and events. It characterized the restriction as informal pastoral safety guidance, not judicial discipline: it did not bar sacraments, worship elsewhere, or transfer, and attendance could resume upon medical assurance. The conditional local restriction therefore remained undisturbed.

title: White v. Siouxlands Presbytery
synopsis: A minister complained that his presbytery wrongly refused to order a BCO 31-2 investigation into another minister’s Covenant of Works/Federal Vision views. The SJC sustained the complaint and remanded for that investigation, holding that BCO 31-2 requires investigation of credible, injurious reports about Christian character. The presbytery erred by applying the higher evidentiary standard for conviction after process; reports sufficient to trigger investigation need not establish guilt or a strong presumption of guilt, and hearsay or conflicting testimony can require investigation rather than justify refusal. A concurrence agreed in result; the dissent found no clear error in the presbytery’s exercise of discretion.

title: Dunn v. Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC held TE Dwight Dunn's complaint administratively out of order under OMSJC 9.1 and directed Presbytery to remedy the deficiencies by its next Stated Meeting before further action under OMSJC 9.2. The original complaint had been transmitted to the Faith Church Commission by the Stated Clerk, not committed by Presbytery motion as BCO 15-3 requires, and after the Commission denied it, the Commission did not seek Presbytery approval of its judgment. Because Presbytery had not acted, the SJC complaint was premature; no merits were reached.

title: Dunn and Pesnell v. Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery
synopsis: The complaint challenged Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery’s November 17, 2012 vote adopting its Complaint Commission’s recommendation to institute process and try TE David Swavely. The SJC did not sustain it. Although the record showed possible procedural irregularities—including unauthorized circulation of an earlier complaint—the SJC found no reversible error: presbyteries receive deference on factual records and broad latitude to judge the sufficiency of investigations. The recommendation to proceed to trial stands, subject to later parliamentary action. The SJC did not decide Swavely’s guilt.

title: Steven Hahn v. Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery
synopsis: Hahn challenged Presbytery’s ruling that CTKPC Session lawfully excluded him from that congregation’s worship until a psychiatric evaluation addressed safety concerns. The SJC denied the complaint. Applying BCO 39-3.3, it found no clear error in the lower courts’ credibility and discretionary judgments, given Session’s familiarity with the people and events. It characterized the restriction as informal pastoral safety guidance, not judicial discipline: it did not bar sacraments, worship elsewhere, or transfer, and attendance could resume upon medical assurance. The conditional local restriction therefore remained undisturbed.

title: Crouse v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
synopsis: A serving deacon nominated for ruling elder complained that his session removed his nomination before BCO 24-1 instruction or examination. The SJC held the session erred by adding an unwritten pre-examination 'vetting' removal and that Northwest Georgia Presbytery erred in approving it: BCO 24-1's sequence—instruction and examination before the session determines eligibility—is mandatory. The ruling reserved the session's sound discretion and the treatment of frivolous or clearly disqualified nominees. The complaint was sustained and remanded for adjudication consistent with the decision.

title: Dudt v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
synopsis: A ruling elder appealed convictions for distributing an SJC decision contrary to Session's will and for allegedly false, divisive statements in an email opposing a pastoral-election proposal. The SJC sustained the appeal, reversed Session and Presbytery in whole, rendered not guilty, removed the indefinite suspension, and restored him to office. Session could not bind conscience without scriptural authority, and no express prohibition or proof of falsity existed. Many other specifications were rejected; a concurrence cautioned that such emails are rarely wise.

title: Woodham v. South Florida Presbytery
synopsis: South Florida Presbytery deposed a Teaching Elder, suspended him from the sacraments, and later excommunicated him without first assigning him to a particular church under BCO 46-8. The complainant argued that omission stripped Presbytery of jurisdiction. The SJC denied the complaint: BCO 46-8 requires assignment but fixes no timeframe or mechanism; a deposed minister remains under Presbytery's jurisdiction until transfer, and BCO 37-9(a) preserves censure authority. Deferring under BCO 39-3, the SJC found no clear error in Presbytery's efforts. Two concurrences agreed in result but disputed the majority's broad reasoning and deference.

title: Nancy A. Conrad et al. v. Central Carolina Presbytery
synopsis: After a Session corrected an earlier unauthorized removal from its rolls, then formally voted to remove the same members, the members challenged Presbytery's denial of their complaint, arguing that the new removal defied the prior decision. The ruling left the later membership removal undisturbed.

title: Baer v. Illiana Presbytery
synopsis: An appeal from a Presbytery judgment and indefinite suspension of a pastor turned on whether he violated the Ninth Commandment and ordination/installation vows by telling the congregation the Session had 'demanded' his resignation for six weeks. The SJC denied the appeal, holding the Session as a whole had not formally demanded resignation; individual elders' earlier opinions did not excuse the overstatement, which harmed the Session's good name. It also found no due-process irregularity or prejudice warranting reversal, deferring to the lower court under BCO 39-3, leaving indefinite suspension in place.

title: Dale Cutler v. Platte Valley Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC found that Presbytery of Siouxlands erred in denying a complaint that sought the appointment of a committee to conduct a BCO 31-2 investigation into whether TE Greg Lawrence held or taught views associated with Federal Vision theology contrary to the PCA's doctrinal standards. title: Hutchinson & Bulkeley v. Western Carolina
synopsis: The complaint challenged Presbytery’s commissions and its response to a canceled congregational meeting. The SJC upheld the Inman Commission because a Session may reference limited duties without congregational consent. It sustained the challenges to Presbytery’s consideration of the August 7 meeting and appointment of the Sealy Commission because the Session majority had validly canceled the meeting. Linton’s and Pellom’s calls therefore remained undissolved and Neville was uncalled, absent later congregational action. The SJC also upheld Presbytery’s criticism of the cancellation as unwise and its refusal to issue a BCO 40-5 citation.

title: Dale Cutler v. Platte Valley Presbytery

title: White v. Siouxlands Presbytery
synopsis: A minister complained that his presbytery wrongly refused to order a BCO 31-2 investigation into another minister’s Covenant of Works/Federal Vision views. The SJC sustained the complaint and remanded for that investigation, holding that BCO 31-2 requires investigation of credible, injurious reports about Christian character. The presbytery erred by applying the higher evidentiary standard for conviction after process; reports sufficient to trigger investigation need not establish guilt or a strong presumption of guilt, and hearsay or conflicting testimony can require investigation rather than justify refusal. A concurrence agreed in result; the dissent found no clear error in the presbytery’s exercise of discretion.

title: Doty v. Nashville Presbytery
synopsis: A complainant challenged Nashville Presbytery's handling of allegations against a teaching elder. The SJC held the matter judicially out of order and dismissed it, finding the original filing with the church session was not a BCO 43-1 complaint because the session lacked jurisdiction over the teaching elder. Presbytery properly treated the allegations as BCO 31-2/34-1 reports, and the complainant, not a Nashville member, lacked standing to complain about that new action. A nine-member dissent argued the filing of charges conferred standing under prior SJC cases.

title: Fordice v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery

It sustained the complaint, annulled the denial, and remanded for Presbytery to amend the documents, institute process, reactivate the investigative committee, or otherwise respond directly and specifically to the unresolved allegations.

title: Crouse v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
synopsis: A serving deacon nominated for ruling elder complained that his session removed his nomination before BCO 24-1 instruction or examination. The SJC held the session erred by adding an unwritten pre-examination 'vetting' removal and that Northwest Georgia Presbytery erred in approving it: BCO 24-1's sequence—instruction and examination before the session determines eligibility—is mandatory. The ruling reserved the session's sound discretion and the treatment of frivolous or clearly disqualified nominees. The complaint was sustained and remanded for adjudication consistent with the decision.

Session could not bind conscience without scriptural authority, and no express prohibition or proof of falsity existed. Many other specifications were rejected; a concurrence cautioned that such emails are rarely wise.

title: Doty v. Nashville Presbytery
synopsis: A complainant challenged Nashville Presbytery's handling of allegations against a teaching elder. The SJC held the matter judicially out of order and dismissed it, finding the original filing with the church session was not a BCO 43-1 complaint because the session lacked jurisdiction over the teaching elder. Presbytery properly treated the allegations as BCO 31-2/34-1 reports, and the complainant, not a Nashville member, lacked standing to complain about that new action. A nine-member dissent argued the filing of charges conferred standing under prior SJC cases.

title: Fordice v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery
synopsis: A church member challenged Presbytery’s denial of his complaint after it resolved accusations against a minister through a BCO 38-1 confession rather than trial. The SJC held that using confession without process was not itself error, but the statement and confession failed to correlate with and address the specific allegations. It sustained the complaint, annulled the denial, and remanded for Presbytery to amend the documents, institute process, reactivate the investigative committee, or otherwise respond directly and specifically to the unresolved allegations.

title: Troxell v. Presbytery of the Southwest
synopsis: A complaint challenged Presbytery’s institution of two charges against a teaching elder and related pretrial actions. The SJC annulled the household-management charge because process began fifteen months after the alleged offense and the record showed no recently flagrant, newly evident, or continuing offense under BCO 32-20. It also held that declaring the elder not in good standing removed rights without process, but left his properly imposed suspension effective. It rejected objections to discussion, questioning, and the timely submission charge, which could proceed without any determination of guilt.

title: Crouse v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
synopsis: A serving deacon nominated for ruling elder complained that his session removed his nomination before BCO 24-1 instruction or examination. The SJC held the session erred by adding an unwritten pre-examination 'vetting' removal and that Northwest Georgia Presbytery erred in approving it: BCO 24-1's sequence—instruction and examination before the session determines eligibility—is mandatory. The ruling reserved the session's sound discretion and the treatment of frivolous or clearly disqualified nominees. The complaint was sustained and remanded for adjudication consistent with the decision.

title: Ganzel v. Central Florida Presbytery
synopsis: A minister appealed a judgment finding him guilty on most charges and imposing six months’ suspension. The SJC held BCO 32-20 barred Specifications 1, 2, and 4 because Presbytery lacked extraordinary justification for prosecuting old allegations, but did not bar ongoing Specification 3. It separately found the entire process constitutionally flawed and prejudicial. The SJC reversed the whole censure, declined Presbytery’s requested harsher sentence, and concluded the matter. A concurrence disputed the majority’s BCO 32-20 interpretation while agreeing with the result.

The remand permitted a constitutionally compliant trial; it did not resolve guilt or bar discipline.

title: Nickoley v. Rocky Mountain
synopsis: Rocky Mountain Presbytery cited Pastor Bruce Nickoley for contumacy during his trial, after he allegedly refused to tell his congregation to stop picketing, and immediately deposed him without a hearing. On appeal, the SJC sustained the appeal, holding the Presbytery misapplied BCO provisions on confession, citation, refusal to testify, and deposition; Nickoley neither confessed nor refused to appear. Although presbyteries have general authority to maintain order, serious charges require due process. The SJC remanded, recommending either a new process beginning with BCO §32-3 or revocation of the deposition and reinstatement.

title: Charles Kim v. Korean Capital Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC addressed whether a presbytery and its administrative/judicial commission could suspend a local session and assume original jurisdiction over charges against a ruling elder. It answered no: original jurisdiction belonged to the session, and a presbytery cannot "act for" a lower court by replacing congregationally elected elders. Preliminary Principle Six, BCO 16-2, and BCO 31-1/33-1 controlled; the commission's interpretation of BCO 13-9 conflicted with those principles. The Presbytery's and Commission's actions, including the censure approved by Presbytery, were reversed.

title: Sang Bai Kim and RE Chan Soo Kim v. Korean Eastern Presbytery
synopsis: In a dispute arising from a Korean Eastern Presbytery congregational election, two ruling elders were tried, refused to plead, and were suspended from sacraments and office; KEP denied their appeal, then increased the censures to deposition and excommunication for contumacy. The SJC affirmed KEP's denial and the guilt findings, but reversed the increased censures. An appellate court may not increase a censure under BCO 42-9; the trial court retains discretion to remove or increase an indefinite suspension, though the appellate court may recommend a lesser censure. The original suspension remained.

title: Session of Delhi Presbyterian Church v. Louisiana Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC sustained a session's timely complaint that Louisiana Presbytery barred one of its members from the Lord's Table after assuming original jurisdiction. Under BCO 33-1, a presbytery may assume jurisdiction only when the session 'refuses to act'; because the session had investigated and found no strong presumption of guilt, it acted, so LAP never acquired jurisdiction. The censure was therefore a nullity, and the member remained under his session. The SJC also held the jurisdictional assumption reviewable despite no timely complaint against it. Three commissioners dissented.

synopsis: Smith challenged Presbytery’s reversal of a finding that an elder’s race-and-IQ views did not create a strong presumption of guilt and its immediate judgment against those views. The SJC upheld the reversal as a discretionary determination, without addressing its merits, but annulled the declaration against the views because a strong-presumption finding required judicial process. title: Hardie v. Metro Atlanta Presbytery
synopsis: TE John Hardie appealed his Metro Atlanta Presbytery conviction on three charges of breaking ordination vows and indefinite suspension, alleging seventeen procedural and evidentiary errors. Applying BCO 39-2/3 clear-error deference, the SJC denied every specification and upheld the judgment and censure. It found no clear error in the BCO 31-2 investigation, indictment/prosecutor process, commission membership, evidence rulings, scheduling, alleged prejudice, or censure. It assessed transcription costs equally while encouraging MAP to absorb them, and cautioned that an absent commissioner's vote might support a future challenge.

title: Presbyterian Church in America v. South Florida Presbytery (Citation)
synopsis: Reviewing South Florida Presbytery’s response to a General Assembly citation, the SJC found most responses satisfactory but rejected one because it did not address BCO 32-2’s requirement to proceed once a charge is made. It approved previously unsubmitted 2009 executive-session minutes with an exception because their treatment of a teaching elder appeared to violate BCO 46-8. Presbytery also had to submit amended minutes and complete, or formally plan, overdue Session-record reviews for report to the 45th General Assembly.

title: Doty v. Nashville Presbytery
synopsis: A complainant challenged Nashville Presbytery's handling of allegations against a teaching elder. The SJC held the matter judicially out of order and dismissed it, finding the original filing with the church session was not a BCO 43-1 complaint because the session lacked jurisdiction over the teaching elder. Presbytery properly treated the allegations as BCO 31-2/34-1 reports, and the complainant, not a Nashville member, lacked standing to complain about that new action. A nine-member dissent argued the filing of charges conferred standing under prior SJC cases.

title: Fordice v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery

It sustained the complaint, annulled the denial, and remanded for Presbytery to amend the documents, institute process, reactivate the investigative committee, or otherwise respond directly and specifically to the unresolved allegations.

title: Harrell et al. v. Covenant Presbytery

The ruling addressed neither the allegations’ merits nor all old charges categorically.

The censure was therefore a nullity, and the member remained under his session. The SJC also held the jurisdictional assumption reviewable despite no timely complaint against it. title: Nickoley v. Rocky Mountain
synopsis: Rocky Mountain Presbytery cited Pastor Bruce Nickoley for contumacy during his trial, after he allegedly refused to tell his congregation to stop picketing, and immediately deposed him without a hearing. On appeal, the SJC sustained the appeal, holding the Presbytery misapplied BCO provisions on confession, citation, refusal to testify, and deposition; Nickoley neither confessed nor refused to appear. Although presbyteries have general authority to maintain order, serious charges require due process. The SJC remanded, recommending either a new process beginning with BCO §32-3 or revocation of the deposition and reinstatement.

title: Nickoley v. Rocky Mountain
synopsis: Bruce Nickoley complained against Rocky Mountain Presbytery over its action dissolving the relationship with Evergreen Church. The SJC held the complaint administratively out of order under SJC Manual 10.1. The same matter was already the subject of an appeal granted to Evergreen Church and docketed for Presbytery's January 22–24, 1997 meeting, and BCO 43-1 provides that no complaint is allowable in a judicial case in which an appeal is taken. No merits ruling was reached.

title: Smith v. Southwest Presbytery
synopsis: Smith appealed discipline for divisiveness, gossip and slander, broken membership vows, and contumacy arising largely from complaints and letters during church conflict. The SJC sustained her appeal, reversed guilt on all four charges, and annulled suspension from the sacraments. The documentary record proved none of the allegations; filing complaints was not itself divisiveness, and the trial improperly lacked a witness, shifted proof to Smith, showed prejudice, and unfairly rejected her written defense. The SJC declined remand because the evidence was insufficient.

title: Sang Bai Kim and RE Chan Soo Kim v. Korean Eastern Presbytery
synopsis: In a dispute arising from a Korean Eastern Presbytery congregational election, two ruling elders were tried, refused to plead, and were suspended from sacraments and office; KEP denied their appeal, then increased the censures to deposition and excommunication for contumacy. The SJC affirmed KEP's denial and the guilt findings, but reversed the increased censures. An appellate court may not increase a censure under BCO 42-9; the trial court retains discretion to remove or increase an indefinite suspension, though the appellate court may recommend a lesser censure. The original suspension remained.

title: Plowman v. Philadelphia Presbytery
synopsis: A church session suspended a member from the Lord's Table and found her guilty of contumacy. The chairman of Presbytery's Judicial Business Committee advised her that her appeal was out of order; Presbytery later ruled her complaint untimely. The SJC sustained her complaint: she had submitted to regular trial, making her appeal in order under BCO 42-2, and her complaint was timely after Presbytery's advice caused the appeal to be renamed. It remanded for Presbytery to adjudicate the appeal. Filing the appeal suspended the Lord's Table censure pending final adjudication; the SJC questioned the contumacy ruling.

title: Kim v. Korean Eastern Presbytery

It sustained deposition but found excommunication excessive given the conflict and replaced it with indefinite suspension from the sacraments. It did not sustain the threat conviction because the attorney’s letter was absent from the record. A dissent disputed the contumacy ruling.

title: Ruff v. Nashville Presbytery

title: Sartorius v. Siouxlands Presbytery
synopsis: Did a presbytery fail in its duty to condemn erroneous opinions by acquitting a minister on theological-error charges? The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the acquittal undisturbed. A complaint against a not-guilty verdict cannot provoke a retrial at the superior court; under BCO 43 the superior court may only annul or remand, not reverse, and the complainant bore the burden to show error from the record. The record contained the defendant's testimony, including recantations or clarifications, Defense Exhibit 1, and witness testimony sufficient to refrain from contradicting the trial court. The SJC expressly did not decide the defendant's actual views. A separate concurrence elaborated deference standards but did not change the judgment.

title: Crouse v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
synopsis: A serving deacon nominated for ruling elder complained that his session removed his nomination before BCO 24-1 instruction or examination. The SJC held the session erred by adding an unwritten pre-examination 'vetting' removal and that Northwest Georgia Presbytery erred in approving it: BCO 24-1's sequence—instruction and examination before the session determines eligibility—is mandatory. The ruling reserved the session's sound discretion and the treatment of frivolous or clearly disqualified nominees. The complaint was sustained and remanded for adjudication consistent with the decision.

title: Dudt v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery

The SJC sustained the appeal, reversed Session and Presbytery in whole, rendered not guilty, removed the indefinite suspension, and restored him to office. Session could not bind conscience without scriptural authority, and no express prohibition or proof of falsity existed. Many other specifications were rejected; a concurrence cautioned that such emails are rarely wise.

title: Steven Hahn v. Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery
synopsis: Hahn challenged Presbytery’s ruling that CTKPC Session lawfully excluded him from that congregation’s worship until a psychiatric evaluation addressed safety concerns. It characterized the restriction as informal pastoral safety guidance, not judicial discipline: it did not bar sacraments, worship elsewhere, or transfer, and attendance could resume upon medical assurance. The conditional local restriction therefore remained undisturbed.

Presbytery properly treated the allegations as BCO 31-2/34-1 reports, and the complainant, not a Nashville member, lacked standing to complain about that new action. A nine-member dissent argued the filing of charges conferred standing under prior SJC cases.

title: Crouse v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
synopsis: A serving deacon nominated for ruling elder complained that his session removed his nomination before BCO 24-1 instruction or examination. The SJC held the session erred by adding an unwritten pre-examination 'vetting' removal and that Northwest Georgia Presbytery erred in approving it: BCO 24-1's sequence—instruction and examination before the session determines eligibility—is mandatory. The ruling reserved the session's sound discretion and the treatment of frivolous or clearly disqualified nominees. The complaint was sustained and remanded for adjudication consistent with the decision.

title: Crouse v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
synopsis: A complaint challenging a session's refusal to advance an ordained deacon's nomination for re-election to the diaconate was denied by the SJC. Northwest Georgia Presbytery had adopted its judicial commission's judgment that the session did not err; applying BCO 39-3(3)'s deference to discretionary judgments, the SJC found no clear error, held formal charges were unnecessary and re-election was not guaranteed, and refused to attribute one elder's questionable retaliation rationale to the session. The majority encouraged prompt communication of reasons. A dissent would apply BCO 39-3.4 and sustain.

title: Dudt v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
synopsis: A ruling elder appealed convictions for distributing an SJC decision contrary to Session's will and for allegedly false, divisive statements in an email opposing a pastoral-election proposal. The SJC sustained the appeal, reversed Session and Presbytery in whole, rendered not guilty, removed the indefinite suspension, and restored him to office. Session could not bind conscience without scriptural authority, and no express prohibition or proof of falsity existed. Many other specifications were rejected; a concurrence cautioned that such emails are rarely wise.

title: Speck v. Missouri Presbytery
synopsis: Ryan Speck challenged Missouri Presbytery’s BCO 31-2 investigation and its refusal to commence process against Greg Johnson on four allegations concerning same-sex attraction as sin, identity in Christ, sanctification, and fitness for office. The SJC denied the complaint in full. It found no clear procedural error and held that Johnson’s explanations and clarifications made Presbytery’s non-indictment judgments reasonable. No trial was ordered. The ruling neither adjudged Johnson guilty nor endorsed every statement or broader constitutional position concerning same-sex attraction.

title: Biese et al. v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery
synopsis: Biese and others complained that Tennessee Valley Presbytery erred by approving Redeemer Church session minutes without exception—minutes noting a youth Super Bowl party—and by denying their complaint seeking a Sabbath exception. The SJC denied the complaint: because Presbytery gave no reasons for its actions, the record was insufficient to find it erred in interpreting the Constitution. A concurrence said the denial did not decide the Sabbath merits; a dissent would have held the complaint judicially out of order for lack of SJC jurisdiction over presbytery record review.

title: Huffman v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery

The SJC found it judicially out of order because the case began and was nearly completed when the former rule provided review by complaint, and retroactive application would be unfair. It remanded for Presbytery to adjudicate the filing as a complaint at its next stated meeting; denial or failure to act permits review by the SJC. No merits issue was decided.

The SJC left unresolved deposition from office when excommunication is absent.

The SJC sustained the complaint by reference to its decision in Case 2008-15, Issue 5, holding that Presbytery erred in appointing the Sealy Commission in the first place since the underlying August 7 congregational meeting was illegitimate.

title: Meyerhoff v. Chesapeake Presbytery
synopsis: Meyerhoff challenged Chesapeake Presbytery’s called meeting to receive, discuss, and entertain questions about an original-jurisdiction commission’s initial report. Without deciding whether those actions were procedurally erroneous, the SJC held the complaint moot in view of its judgment in Case 2008-11. It directed Presbytery to note the mootness ruling in the minutes of the August 16, 2008 meeting.

title: Morton H. Smith v. Western Carolina Presbytery
synopsis: The complaint challenged Presbytery’s commissions and its response to a canceled congregational meeting. The SJC upheld the Inman Commission because a Session may reference limited duties without congregational consent. It sustained the challenges to Presbytery’s consideration of the August 7 meeting and appointment of the Sealy Commission because the Session majority had validly canceled the meeting. Linton’s and Pellom’s calls therefore remained undissolved and Neville was uncalled, absent later congregational action. The SJC also upheld Presbytery’s criticism of the cancellation as unwise and its refusal to issue a BCO 40-5 citation.

title: Koerkenmeier v. Illiana Presbytery
synopsis: Illiana Presbytery appointed a commission with broad power 'to deal with matters' at Center Grove Presbyterian Church after a pastor requested inquiry into alleged evils. The SJC sustained the complaint but held the error harmless: the broad charge could take original jurisdiction from the session contrary to BCO 11-3 & 4 and 33-1, while a limited investigative committee under BCO 13-9(f) and 31-2 would have been proper. Because the commission never exercised that power and the session endorsed its findings, no remedy, including invalidation of the adopted report, was ordered.

title: Bethel v. Southeast Alabama Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC held Complaint 2012-06 administratively out of order because it was not filed within thirty days (BCO 43-2; OMSJC 18.10.b) and because the complainant, a Deacon who was not a commissioner to Presbytery at the time of the challenged action, lacked standing (BCO 43-1). No merits review appears; the adopted vote was 18 concurring, 2 not qualified, and 4 absent.

title: Steven Hahn v. Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery
synopsis: Steven Hahn filed multiple complaints against Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery (PMWP) arising from his exclusion from worship at Christ the King Presbyterian Church pending a psychiatric evaluation, his subsequent conviction of three charges by PMWP, and PMWP's refusal to institute process against those he accused. The SJC denied all three complaints (2011-11, 2011-12, 2011-15), finding no clear error in PMWP's exercise of deference to the lower court, guilty verdict, or declination to appoint a prosecutor under BCO 31-8.

title: Steven Hahn v. Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery
synopsis: Hahn challenged Presbytery’s ruling that CTKPC Session lawfully excluded him from that congregation’s worship until a psychiatric evaluation addressed safety concerns. The SJC denied the complaint. Applying BCO 39-3.3, it found no clear error in the lower courts’ credibility and discretionary judgments, given Session’s familiarity with the people and events. It characterized the restriction as informal pastoral safety guidance, not judicial discipline: it did not bar sacraments, worship elsewhere, or transfer, and attendance could resume upon medical assurance. The conditional local restriction therefore remained undisturbed.

The SJC denied the complaint: because Presbytery gave no reasons for its actions, the record was insufficient to find it erred in interpreting the Constitution. A concurrence said the denial did not decide the Sabbath merits; a dissent would have held the complaint judicially out of order for lack of SJC jurisdiction over presbytery record review.

title: Woodham v. South Florida Presbytery
synopsis: South Florida Presbytery deposed a Teaching Elder, suspended him from the sacraments, and later excommunicated him without first assigning him to a particular church under BCO 46-8. The complainant argued that omission stripped Presbytery of jurisdiction. The SJC denied the complaint: BCO 46-8 requires assignment but fixes no timeframe or mechanism; a deposed minister remains under Presbytery's jurisdiction until transfer, and BCO 37-9(a) preserves censure authority. Deferring under BCO 39-3, the SJC found no clear error in Presbytery's efforts. Two concurrences agreed in result but disputed the majority's broad reasoning and deference.

title: Smith v. Southwest Presbytery
synopsis: Smith appealed discipline for divisiveness, gossip and slander, broken membership vows, and contumacy arising largely from complaints and letters during church conflict. The SJC sustained her appeal, reversed guilt on all four charges, and annulled suspension from the sacraments. The documentary record proved none of the allegations; filing complaints was not itself divisiveness, and the trial improperly lacked a witness, shifted proof to Smith, showed prejudice, and unfairly rejected her written defense. The SJC declined remand because the evidence was insufficient.

title: Anthony Dallison v. North Florida Presbytery
synopsis: After TE Anthony Dallison confessed spousal abuse and received an indefinite suspension, North Florida Presbytery later found him impenitent and deposed him and suspended him from the sacraments. Dallison complained that increasing the censure required fresh charges and trial. The SJC disagreed: his BCO 38-1 confession waived trial rights as to the original charge; the offender then had to satisfy the court of repentance, and the presbytery could investigate and impose higher censure under BCO 37-3, 37-4, 37-8, and 34-4b. The complaint was not sustained.

title: Plowman v. Philadelphia Presbytery
synopsis: A church session suspended a member from the Lord's Table and found her guilty of contumacy. The chairman of Presbytery's Judicial Business Committee advised her that her appeal was out of order; Presbytery later ruled her complaint untimely. The SJC sustained her complaint: she had submitted to regular trial, making her appeal in order under BCO 42-2, and her complaint was timely after Presbytery's advice caused the appeal to be renamed. It remanded for Presbytery to adjudicate the appeal. Filing the appeal suspended the Lord's Table censure pending final adjudication; the SJC questioned the contumacy ruling.

title: Paul W. Lee v. Korean Southwest
synopsis: A minister appealed three convictions and suspension that would automatically become indefinite absent repentance. The SJC sustained the appeal: unauthorized committee citations and admonition without process could not support guilt, and multiple trial violations were fatally prejudicial. It set aside the judgment, dismissed the citation and admonition charges, and revoked both censures. The inappropriate-language charge was not adjudicated on its merits; Presbytery could retry it on remand or dismiss it.

title: Kim v. Korean Eastern Presbytery
synopsis: A minister appealed convictions for contumacy and threatening elders with civil litigation, plus deposition and excommunication. The SJC sustained contumacy as failure to remain subject to the brethren under the ordination vow, not BCO 32-6-type contumacy. It sustained deposition but found excommunication excessive given the conflict and replaced it with indefinite suspension from the sacraments. It did not sustain the threat conviction because the attorney’s letter was absent from the record. A dissent disputed the contumacy ruling.

title: Kim v. Korean Eastern Presbytery (Complaint)
synopsis: A minister challenged Presbytery’s denial of his complaints concerning a congregational petition and an Administrative Commission’s actions. The SJC sustained both issues: the petition should first have gone to the Session, and Presbytery and its Commission committed additional constitutional errors. Those errors did not excuse his refusal to obey Presbytery, however. Because he had been deposed in Case 2005-8, further action was moot; the SJC granted no remedy, vacatur, or remand.

title: Sherfey v. James River Presbytery
synopsis: Sherfey challenged James River Presbytery’s denial of his complaint and alleged errors in its commission’s proceedings. The SJC ruled the complaint judicially out of order with incurable defects: several grounds had not first been adjudicated by Presbytery as BCO 43-2 required, and the General Assembly filing missed BCO 43-3’s thirty-day deadline. Incorrect advice from Presbytery’s clerk did not excuse compliance. The adopted decision neither reached the merits nor ordered a remand; only a concurrence proposed returning the matter to Presbytery.

title: Keating v. Warrior Presbytery
synopsis: Keating challenged Warrior Presbytery’s decision to divest him of ordination without censure while he was absent. The SJC sustained his appeal, reversed and voided the divestiture, and remanded because BCO 34-10’s required opportunity to be heard in his defense was not provided; this also amounted to hurrying before all testimony was taken. It rejected the reasonable-indulgence claim because Presbytery did not know of his postponement request. Keating remained a minister in good standing, but Presbytery could reconsider divestiture after reasonably soliciting a defense.

title: Sawyers et al. v. Missouri Presbytery
synopsis: Elders complained that Missouri Presbytery erred in its BCO 31-2 investigation by finding insufficient evidence to raise a strong presumption of guilt that TE Jeffrey Meyers held Federal Vision views contrary to the Westminster Standards. The SJC answered yes: MOP erred under BCO 34-5, and the ordinary remedy was compliance with BCO 31-2. But because MOP had already tried Meyers on April 13–14, 2012, the SJC held further action moot, ordering no additional relief. Adopted by the SJC as a whole, with one dissent.

title: Smith v. Mississippi Valley Presbytery

The SJC rejected four allegations and most of the fifth, holding among other things that two ignored citations are only one possible form of contumacy. It sustained the complaint solely because Presbytery wrongly treated Smith's absence as a refusal to appear: a committee email was not a citation by Presbytery. The SJC reversed that finding but did not annul the excommunication, leaving Presbytery to consider whether modification was necessary.

title: Doty v. Nashville Presbytery

Presbytery properly treated the allegations as BCO 31-2/34-1 reports, and the complainant, not a Nashville member, lacked standing to complain about that new action. A nine-member dissent argued the filing of charges conferred standing under prior SJC cases.

title: Dodson et al. v. Ohio Presbytery

Presbytery nevertheless had to impose an appropriate lesser censure or remand for one, and lacked authority to mandate transfer to another church. The unappealed heresy convictions remained, but because the members had joined another church, further proceedings were moot.

title: Jeffrey M. Black v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery

title: McNeil v. Chesapeake Presbytery
synopsis: An appellant under suspension from the sacraments challenged the presbytery's judicial commission process and censure. The SJC held the appeal judicially out of order—not decided on the merits—because he had not submitted to a regular trial, as BCO 42-2 requires. Treated as a complaint, it was also out of order: it had not first been presented to the presbytery, and the 30-day period had expired. title: Sang Soo Ryoo v. Korean Capital Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC sustained an assistant pastor’s appeal from a three-year suspension from the sacraments after a Korean Capital Presbytery commission found him guilty of participating in the call of an allegedly unconstitutional presbytery meeting. The decisive defect was procedural: no indictment was served, no prosecutor was clearly appointed, and no trial minutes appeared in the record; service of an indictment with a witness list was critical. The case was remanded for a new trial, and the SJC expressly did not reach the merits or citation adequacy.

title: Lyons v. Western Carolina Presbytery
synopsis: Kirk Lyons filed BCO 32-2 charges against TE Craig Bulkeley with Western Carolina Presbytery. WCP dismissed the charges, then ruled Lyons's complaint administratively out of order for lack of standing. The SJC answered that the dismissal was not erroneous—Presbytery had discretion under BCO 31-8, 34-2, and 32-20, and the record showed no clear error—but that WCP erred on standing because Lyons's filing brought him under its jurisdiction. Because that error was not prejudicial, the SJC denied the complaint.

title: Charles Tarter v. Evangel Presbytery
synopsis: A teaching elder appealed his judgment and deposition for refusing Presbytery committee directives and allegedly avoiding accountability. The SJC sustained five of nine specifications, holding that the committee could not impose requirements lacking constitutional warrant or control an independent mission board; vague allegations and testimony unavailable for cross-examination also impaired the trial. Because the record did not prove an ongoing pattern of insubordination, it vacated the censure and remanded for a constitutionally compliant proceeding or dismissal. Three specifications failed, while one duplicated another.

It also said pertinent questions about whether a call is for the good of the Church may be asked, but agreed the amends—including removing TE Hsu—were inappropriate and could not rescind his installation.

title: Robert D. Hopper v. James River Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC denied Hopper's complaint against James River Presbytery's April 13, 1991 order barring him from teaching or preaching his views on prophecy and tongues. It rejected all five specifications: Scripture did not forbid the order; the 1974 Pastoral Letter did not address presbytery's power to enjoin such teaching; forbearance did not preclude protecting peace and purity; presbytery could restrict preaching short of a heresy finding without binding conscience; and allowing presbyteral discussion while restricting congregational teaching was not inconsistent. The action remained in force.

title: St. Paul Session, et al. v. Central Florida Presbytery
synopsis: The St. Paul Session and other Central Florida presbyters complained that Presbytery wrongly sustained a commission report denying the Session complaint and declining to find a strong presumption of guilt against Pastor John Hutchinson. The SJC denied the complaint on both issues. It held CFP permissibly directed a BCO 31-2 investigation and chose its own procedures; procedural irregularities and possible bias did not show BCO 39-3 clear error, though the panel criticized CFP’s handling. A lone dissent would remand, alleging the commission ignored the substance of 41 of 45 specifications.

title: Western Carolina v. Tennessee Valley
synopsis: Three presbyteries asked the General Assembly under BCO 34-1 to assume original jurisdiction over a minister alleged to have allowed women to preach from a church pulpit. The SJC held the requests administratively out of order and did not reach the allegation’s merits. Worship was the Session’s responsibility, so the minister could not be held liable for actions assigned to it; moreover, Tennessee Valley Presbytery had acted on the allegations, defeating BCO 34-1’s refusal-to-act prerequisite. No further proceedings were ordered.

title: Larry Ball v. Westminster Presbytery
synopsis: A complaint challenged Westminster Presbytery's denial of a challenge to its May 15, 2001 plan to withdraw from the PCA. The SJC answered no: the Presbytery did not err, and denied the complaint. BCO 25's local-church withdrawal right and the BCO Preface's grassroots principles extend to presbyteries unless expressly excluded, so a presbytery may determine its own membership and affiliation. The plan did not 'act for' local churches; they retained rights to remain in the PCA or leave, and retained property and internal operations.

title: Merriam v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC denied TE Stuart H. Merriam's appeal from Tennessee Valley Presbytery's April 20, 2002 conviction on three ordination-vow specifications and its indefinite suspension. It rejected procedural challenges—that the earlier called meeting was improperly convened and that TVP was prejudiced by prior cases—and found no clear error, applying BCO 39-3(2)'s deference to lower-court factual findings. The SJC sustained TVP's judgment; prior SJC Cases 95-10 and 96-7 had only indirect bearing and did not require retrial.

title: Session of Delhi Presbyterian Church v. Louisiana Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC sustained a session's timely complaint that Louisiana Presbytery barred one of its members from the Lord's Table after assuming original jurisdiction. Under BCO 33-1, a presbytery may assume jurisdiction only when the session 'refuses to act'; because the session had investigated and found no strong presumption of guilt, it acted, so LAP never acquired jurisdiction. title: Steven Hahn v. Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery
synopsis: Hahn challenged Presbytery’s ruling that CTKPC Session lawfully excluded him from that congregation’s worship until a psychiatric evaluation addressed safety concerns. The SJC denied the complaint. Applying BCO 39-3.3, it found no clear error in the lower courts’ credibility and discretionary judgments, given Session’s familiarity with the people and events. It characterized the restriction as informal pastoral safety guidance, not judicial discipline: it did not bar sacraments, worship elsewhere, or transfer, and attendance could resume upon medical assurance. The conditional local restriction therefore remained undisturbed.

title: Thompson v. South Florida Presbytery
synopsis: After a Session excommunicated a member without trial for contumacy, the SJC sustained his complaint and annulled the contumacy judgment, excommunication, and later Session and Presbytery actions. No mutually agreed BCO 38-1 confession existed, and declining a confession meeting was not immediately censurable objective contumacy under BCO 32-6; subjective contumacy required confession or trial. He reverted to membership under pending indictment. The SJC did not find the indictment unconstitutional, decide trial guilt, or consider the unpleaded trespass warning.

title: Doty v. Nashville Presbytery
synopsis: A complainant challenged Nashville Presbytery's handling of allegations against a teaching elder. The SJC held the matter judicially out of order and dismissed it, finding the original filing with the church session was not a BCO 43-1 complaint because the session lacked jurisdiction over the teaching elder. Presbytery properly treated the allegations as BCO 31-2/34-1 reports, and the complainant, not a Nashville member, lacked standing to complain about that new action. A nine-member dissent argued the filing of charges conferred standing under prior SJC cases.

title: Fordice v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery

It sustained the complaint, annulled the denial, and remanded for Presbytery to amend the documents, institute process, reactivate the investigative committee, or otherwise respond directly and specifically to the unresolved allegations.

title: Gonzales v. Great Lakes Presbytery

It also said pertinent questions about whether a call is for the good of the Church may be asked, but agreed the amends—including removing TE Hsu—were inappropriate and could not rescind his installation.

title: Stuart Merriam v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery (Appeal)

The remand permitted a constitutionally compliant trial; it did not resolve guilt or bar discipline.

title: Sung Keon Kim v. Korean Capital Presbytery
synopsis: On appeal from a minister’s deposition in a conflicted Korean Capital Presbytery church, the SJC asked whether the commission followed BCO procedures in instituting and conducting judicial process. The SJC remanded to Presbytery for a new trial under BCO 32 and 34. It expressly did not rule on the adequacy of the citations or the merits.

title: Charles Kim v. Korean Capital Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC addressed whether a presbytery and its administrative/judicial commission could suspend a local session and assume original jurisdiction over charges against a ruling elder. It answered no: original jurisdiction belonged to the session, and a presbytery cannot "act for" a lower court by replacing congregationally elected elders. Preliminary Principle Six, BCO 16-2, and BCO 31-1/33-1 controlled; the commission's interpretation of BCO 13-9 conflicted with those principles. The Presbytery's and Commission's actions, including the censure approved by Presbytery, were reversed.

The dismissal did not erase concerns about undocumented doctrinal findings; those failures were covered by Specification 2. On Presbytery’s guilty plea to that specification, the SJC imposed a public admonition for failing to find a strong presumption of doctrinal guilt and pursue trial. Wilkins’s and his church’s withdrawal made practical amends unavailable.

title: Aven v. Ohio Valley Presbytery

title: Morton H. Smith v. Western Carolina Presbytery
synopsis: The complaint challenged Presbytery’s commissions and its response to a canceled congregational meeting. The SJC upheld the Inman Commission because a Session may reference limited duties without congregational consent. It sustained the challenges to Presbytery’s consideration of the August 7 meeting and appointment of the Sealy Commission because the Session majority had validly canceled the meeting. Linton’s and Pellom’s calls therefore remained undissolved and Neville was uncalled, absent later congregational action. The SJC also upheld Presbytery’s criticism of the cancellation as unwise and its refusal to issue a BCO 40-5 citation.

The SJC sustained the complaint, holding that Presbytery had not proceeded with the required caution and that a bare majority could not demonstrate BCO 34-8’s required strongly favorable general sentiment. It declined to require reordination, calling that question unsettled and treating BCO 37-5’s restoration pronouncement as sufficient pending clarification. The SJC annulled Presbytery’s actions concerning the minister and remanded for a proper probationary and review process.

title: Sherfey v. James River Presbytery
synopsis: Sherfey challenged James River Presbytery’s denial of his complaint and alleged errors in its commission’s proceedings. The SJC ruled the complaint judicially out of order with incurable defects: several grounds had not first been adjudicated by Presbytery as BCO 43-2 required, and the General Assembly filing missed BCO 43-3’s thirty-day deadline. Incorrect advice from Presbytery’s clerk did not excuse compliance. The adopted decision neither reached the merits nor ordered a remand; only a concurrence proposed returning the matter to Presbytery.

title: Gonzales v. Great Lakes Presbytery
synopsis: A minister appealed Great Lakes Presbytery’s divestiture of his office without censure under BCO 34-10. The SJC sustained his claim that Presbytery failed to make required findings that he habitually neglected official functions and that any neglect arose only from lack of acceptance to the Church. It reversed and annulled the divestiture, leaving him a member in good standing, and required no further action. The other four specifications were moot. Presbytery remained free to pursue proper Chapter 31 process or a procedurally compliant BCO 34-10 divestiture.

title: Psiaki v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC sustained Psiaki’s complaint and held that the CPC Session erred by ordaining and installing officers elected at a February 5, 2023 congregational meeting where the congregation’s bylaw excluded communing members under 18 from voting. title: Dale Cutler v. Platte Valley Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC found that Presbytery of Siouxlands erred in denying a complaint that sought the appointment of a committee to conduct a BCO 31-2 investigation into whether TE Greg Lawrence held or taught views associated with Federal Vision theology contrary to the PCA's doctrinal standards. The Court directed that the presbytery conduct the required investigation and established that credible reports affecting Christian character warrant investigation regardless of the evidentiary standards required for conviction.

title: Peter Yuan v. South Coast Presbytery
synopsis: An appeal by Peter Yuan to the Standing Judicial Commission of PCA regarding charges of heresy against Samuel Ling. The case was found to be administratively out of order and did not proceed to a substantive decision on the merits.

title: White v. Siouxlands Presbytery
synopsis: A minister complained that his presbytery wrongly refused to order a BCO 31-2 investigation into another minister’s Covenant of Works/Federal Vision views. The SJC sustained the complaint and remanded for that investigation, holding that BCO 31-2 requires investigation of credible, injurious reports about Christian character. The presbytery erred by applying the higher evidentiary standard for conviction after process; reports sufficient to trigger investigation need not establish guilt or a strong presumption of guilt, and hearsay or conflicting testimony can require investigation rather than justify refusal. A concurrence agreed in result; the dissent found no clear error in the presbytery’s exercise of discretion.

title: Lee v. Korean Eastern Presbytery
synopsis: Korean Eastern Presbytery dismissed TE Eliot Lee's charges against two teaching elders without trial, and the SJC sustained Lee's complaint that this was unconstitutional. Although a presbytery may dismiss charges under BCO 29-1, 32-20, 34-2, or 31-8, it bears the burden of documenting that basis; KEP did not. The SJC refused Lee's request that it enter the guilt verdicts the presbytery should have reached—that power exists on appeal, not complaint. It remanded for KEP to begin process under BCO 32.

title: Art Sartorius et al. v. Siouxlands Presbytery

The SJC sustained the complaint on procedural grounds: the trial commission relied on his post-indictment exculpatory writings while he declined to testify, depriving the prosecution of cross-examination. The SJC ordered a new trial on the same indictment under specified evidentiary procedures. Because this was a complaint rather than an appeal, it did not reverse the acquittals into findings of guilt or decide the doctrinal merits.

Challenges to witness-judges, venue, and refusal to refer were rejected.

title: Nancy A. Conrad et al. v. Central Carolina Presbytery
synopsis: After a Session corrected an earlier unauthorized removal from its rolls, then formally voted to remove the same members, the members challenged Presbytery's denial of their complaint, arguing that the new removal defied the prior decision. It reversed excommunication because the record did not show impenitence or contumacy, which could not be inferred from exercising the right to remain silent. title: Steven Hahn v. Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery
synopsis: Hahn challenged Presbytery’s ruling that CTKPC Session lawfully excluded him from that congregation’s worship until a psychiatric evaluation addressed safety concerns. The conditional local restriction therefore remained undisturbed.

title: Hutchinson & Bulkeley v. Western Carolina
synopsis: The complaint challenged Presbytery’s commissions and its response to a canceled congregational meeting. The SJC upheld the Inman Commission because a Session may reference limited duties without congregational consent. It sustained the challenges to Presbytery’s consideration of the August 7 meeting and appointment of the Sealy Commission because the Session majority had validly canceled the meeting. Linton’s and Pellom’s calls therefore remained undissolved and Neville was uncalled, absent later congregational action. The SJC also upheld Presbytery’s criticism of the cancellation as unwise and its refusal to issue a BCO 40-5 citation.

title: Frazier v. Nashville Presbytery
synopsis: The SJC denied a complaint challenging Nashville Presbytery's decision not to indict a teaching elder for allegedly sinful teaching on homosexuality and same-sex attraction. The adopted judgment held that the 147-page record showed Presbytery fulfilled its BCO 31-2 investigatory duty and did not show it erred in judgment when it declined process; the complaint was denied 20-0-1. Concurring opinions raised concerns about committee recusal, record clarity, and exegetical uses of Scripture, but they were separate and did not alter the denial.

title: Crouse v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
synopsis: A serving deacon nominated for ruling elder complained that his session removed his nomination before BCO 24-1 instruction or examination. The SJC held the session erred by adding an unwritten pre-examination 'vetting' removal and that Northwest Georgia Presbytery erred in approving it: BCO 24-1's sequence—instruction and examination before the session determines eligibility—is mandatory. The ruling reserved the session's sound discretion and the treatment of frivolous or clearly disqualified nominees. The complaint was sustained and remanded for adjudication consistent with the decision.

title: Dodson et al. v. Ohio Presbytery
synopsis: Grace PCA’s Session challenged Ohio Presbytery’s reversal of excommunication for two members convicted of heresy. The SJC partially sustained the complaint: prior indefinite suspension was not constitutionally required, but Presbytery properly found excommunication too severe because the trial record contained no evidence of contumacy. Presbytery nevertheless had to impose an appropriate lesser censure or remand for one, and lacked authority to mandate transfer to another church. The unappealed heresy convictions remained, but because the members had joined another church, further proceedings were moot.

title: Frazier v. Nashville Presbytery

Concurring opinions raised concerns about committee recusal, record clarity, and exegetical uses of Scripture, but they were separate and did not alter the denial.

title: Woodham v. South Florida Presbytery

synopsis: After TE Anthony Dallison confessed spousal abuse and received an indefinite suspension, North Florida Presbytery later found him impenitent and deposed him and suspended him from the sacraments. Dallison complained that increasing the censure required fresh charges and trial. The SJC disagreed: his BCO 38-1 confession waived trial rights as to the original charge; the offender then had to satisfy the court of repentance, and the presbytery could investigate and impose higher censure under BCO 37-3, 37-4, 37-8, and 34-4b. The complaint was not sustained.

title: Jennings v. North Florida Presbytery
synopsis: North Florida Presbytery restored a minister deposed for adultery by a 19–17 vote. The SJC annulled Presbytery’s actions concerning the minister and remanded for a proper probationary and review process.

title: Sherfey v. James River Presbytery
synopsis: Sherfey challenged James River Presbytery’s denial of his complaint and alleged errors in its commission’s proceedings. The SJC ruled the complaint judicially out of order with incurable defects: several grounds had not first been adjudicated by Presbytery as BCO 43-2 required, and the General Assembly filing missed BCO 43-3’s thirty-day deadline. Incorrect advice from Presbytery’s clerk did not excuse compliance. The adopted decision neither reached the merits nor ordered a remand; only a concurrence proposed returning the matter to Presbytery.

title: Myers v. Illiana Presbytery
synopsis: An elder appealed Presbytery’s elevation, without additional process, of suspensions from office and the Sacraments to deposition and excommunication. Elevation required a hearing on incorrigibility and contumacy—with a charge, evidence, plea, and defense—but not a full de novo trial; disagreement with the original verdict alone was insufficient. The SJC left unresolved deposition from office when excommunication is absent.

title: Bowen v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery
synopsis: Bowen challenged Presbytery’s attempt, two years after installation, to rescind its earlier ruling and annul local officers’ elections and ordinations without trial. The SJC sustained the complaint: ordination is perpetual, deposition requires judicial process, and rescission was out of order after implementation; Presbytery likewise could not suspend a local elder without due process. But it affirmed that infant baptism and limited atonement are fundamentals admitting no officer exception. The officers remained in office but doctrinally out of accord; voluntary demission or proper process was advised.

title: Chappell v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery
synopsis: Ruling Elder Chappell complained against Eastern Carolina Presbytery's Commission, which had suspended the session of Fuller Memorial Presbyterian Church and constituted itself as a 'Session Pro Tem' without due process or congregational consent. The SJC sustained the complaint, holding that the BCO grants no authority for a presbytery to depose a session and act in its place, that suspension requires due process, and that the congregation has an inalienable right to be governed by officers it has chosen.

title: Marshall v. Eastern Carolina Presbytery
synopsis: Teaching Elder Wallace Marshall complained against the same Eastern Carolina Presbytery actions at Fuller Memorial Presbyterian Church that were the subject of Case 90-4, filed separately as a Teaching Elder complainant. The SJC sustained this complaint on essentially the same grounds as Case 90-4, finding that the presbytery lacked authority to suspend the session without due process and to constitute itself as a 'Session Pro Tem.'

title: Michael Chastain v. Heritage Presbytery
synopsis: Chastain appealed Heritage Presbytery’s 2006 excommunication and deposition. The SJC held the appeal judicially out of order because Chastain had renounced PCA jurisdiction on May 8, 2006. Consequently, Presbytery’s later proceedings were moot and SJC 2005-1 remained in effect. The SJC did not reach the merits. A concurrence questioned the discipline process after renunciation; a dissent argued the majority lacked constitutional authority to recognize unilateral withdrawal and thereby undercut discipline.

synopsis: A church member challenged Presbytery’s denial of his complaint after it resolved accusations against a minister through a BCO 38-1 confession rather than trial. The SJC held that using confession without process was not itself error, but the statement and confession failed to correlate with and address the specific allegations. It sustained the complaint, annulled the denial, and remanded for Presbytery to amend the documents, institute process, reactivate the investigative committee, or otherwise respond directly and specifically to the unresolved allegations.

title: Crouse v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery
synopsis: A serving deacon nominated for ruling elder complained that his session removed his nomination before BCO 24-1 instruction or examination. The SJC held the session erred by adding an unwritten pre-examination 'vetting' removal and that Northwest Georgia Presbytery erred in approving it: BCO 24-1's sequence—instruction and examination before the session determines eligibility—is mandatory. The ruling reserved the session's sound discretion and the treatment of frivolous or clearly disqualified nominees. The complaint was sustained and remanded for adjudication consistent with the decision.

title: Nickoley v. Rocky Mountain
synopsis: Rocky Mountain Presbytery cited Pastor Bruce Nickoley for contumacy during his trial, after he allegedly refused to tell his congregation to stop picketing, and immediately deposed him without a hearing. On appeal, the SJC sustained the appeal, holding the Presbytery misapplied BCO provisions on confession, citation, refusal to testify, and deposition; Nickoley neither confessed nor refused to appear. Although presbyteries have general authority to maintain order, serious charges require due process. The SJC remanded, recommending either a new process beginning with BCO §32-3 or revocation of the deposition and reinstatement.

No merits ruling was reached.

title: Thornton v. Westminster Presbytery
synopsis: Thornton challenged Westminster Presbytery’s refusal to place Memorial PCA Session’s call in his hands and its simultaneous initiation of administrative divestiture without censure. The SJC sustained both issues, reversed the divestiture decision, and remanded with directions to approve and deliver the call and set an installation date. A valid call supplied the congregational approbation whose absence BCO 34-10’s administrative remedy requires; Presbytery also could not rely on undisclosed concerns while avoiding required judicial process. The ruling found clear error, not an absence of all presbyterial review authority.

title: Eliot Lee v. Korean Eastern Presbytery
synopsis: Lee challenged Korean Eastern Presbytery’s actions affecting his interim pastoral relationship, alleging that its October 3, 2006 meeting lacked a quorum. The SJC held the complaint moot and declared every action taken at that meeting null and void—not merely those concerning his church. The meeting opened with only two ruling elders when three were required, and the minutes did not establish when a quorum was later achieved; its presence therefore could not be presumed.

The SJC upheld the Inman Commission because a Session may reference limited duties without congregational consent. It sustained the challenges to Presbytery’s consideration of the August 7 meeting and appointment of the Sealy Commission because the Session majority had validly canceled the meeting. Linton’s and Pellom’s calls therefore remained undissolved and Neville was uncalled, absent later congregational action. title: Morton Smith v. Western Carolina
synopsis: Smith challenged Presbytery’s reversal of a finding that an elder’s race-and-IQ views did not create a strong presumption of guilt and its immediate judgment against those views. The SJC upheld the reversal as a discretionary determination, without addressing its merits, but annulled the declaration against the views because a strong-presumption finding required judicial process. On remand, Presbytery was to commence process against the elder or rescind that finding and drop the matter. The ruling did not restrict Presbytery’s ability to adopt general position statements outside an investigation.

title: Payne v. Western Carolina Presbytery
synopsis: Four complainants challenged Presbytery’s BCO 31-2 investigation and its finding of no strong presumption of guilt, citing delayed action and failure to interview accusers. The SJC denied the complaints: BCO 31-2 requires due diligence but grants great discretion and prescribes neither interviews nor a timetable, and the record showed no clear constitutional error overcoming deference to Presbytery. Lyons and Woodward also lacked standing because they were not under Presbytery’s jurisdiction. No renewed investigation or process was ordered.

title: Jennings v. North Florida Presbytery
synopsis: North Florida Presbytery restored a minister deposed for adultery by a 19–17 vote. The SJC sustained the complaint, holding that Presbytery had not proceeded with the required caution and that a bare majority could not demonstrate BCO 34-8’s required strongly favorable general sentiment. It declined to require reordination, calling that question unsettled and treating BCO 37-5’s restoration pronouncement as sufficient pending clarification. The SJC annulled Presbytery’s actions concerning the minister and remanded for a proper probationary and review process.

title: Sherfey v. James River Presbytery
synopsis: Sherfey challenged James River Presbytery’s denial of his complaint and alleged errors in its commission’s proceedings. The SJC ruled the complaint judicially out of order with incurable defects: several grounds had not first been adjudicated by Presbytery as BCO 43-2 required, and the General Assembly filing missed BCO 43-3’s thirty-day deadline. Incorrect advice from Presbytery’s clerk did not excuse compliance. The adopted decision neither reached the merits nor ordered a remand; only a concurrence proposed returning the matter to Presbytery.

title: Ruff v. Nashville Presbytery

The SJC sustained the complaint only on the confession and administration of censure: the investigation was adequate and BCO 38-1 was available, but the abstract confession did not acknowledge particular sins against particular people. Presbytery had to amend it, sponsor another reconciliation meeting, document satisfaction with the proceedings, or pursue the matter further, potentially through indictment.

title: Sawyers et al. v. Missouri Presbytery
synopsis: Elders complained that Missouri Presbytery erred in its BCO 31-2 investigation by finding insufficient evidence to raise a strong presumption of guilt that TE Jeffrey Meyers held Federal Vision views contrary to the Westminster Standards. The SJC answered yes: MOP erred under BCO 34-5, and the ordinary remedy was compliance with BCO 31-2. But because MOP had already tried Meyers on April 13–14, 2012, the SJC held further action moot, ordering no additional relief. Adopted by the SJC as a whole, with one dissent.

title: Smith v. Mississippi Valley Presbytery

The SJC rejected four allegations and most of the fifth, holding among other things that two ignored citations are only one possible form of contumacy. It sustained the complaint solely because Presbytery wrongly treated Smith's absence as a refusal to appear: a committee email was not a citation by Presbytery. The SJC reversed that finding but did not annul the excommunication, leaving Presbytery to consider whether modification was necessary.

title: Bumgarner v. Presbytery of the Mississippi Valley
synopsis: A claimant sought BCO 40-5 review of Presbytery’s handling of his earlier judicial case, alleging grossly unconstitutional proceedings and delinquency in failing to investigate his 2012 deposition. The SJC found the application administratively out of order and incapable of being put in order because BCO 40-3 excludes judicial-case proceedings from review and control when notice of appeal or complaint has been given, and he had withdrawn his 2012 complaint acknowledging it could not be resubmitted. It dismissed under OMSJC 9.2(d). The concurrence added that BCO 40 cannot refile a withdrawn complaint or reverse a censure.

title: Thompson v. South Florida Presbytery
synopsis: After a Session excommunicated a member without trial for contumacy, the SJC sustained his complaint and annulled the contumacy judgment, excommunication, and later Session and Presbytery actions. He reverted to membership under pending indictment. The SJC did not find the indictment unconstitutional, decide trial guilt, or consider the unpleaded trespass warning.

The SJC held that using confession without process was not itself error, but the statement and confession failed to correlate with and address the specific allegations. It sustained the complaint, annulled the denial, and remanded for Presbytery to amend the documents, institute process, reactivate the investigative committee, or otherwise respond directly and specifically to the unresolved allegations.

title: Bachmann v. Nashville Presbytery
synopsis: TE James Bachmann appealed Nashville Presbytery's decision to replace his judicial commission's recommended admonition with indefinite suspension. The SJC sustained the appeal: Presbytery violated BCO 15-3 by dividing the verdict and amending the censure, which it had to approve or disapprove as a whole without debate. Bachmann's earlier procedural challenges were not sustained; his unconditional post-trial confession waived them. The SJC rendered the commission's judgment and admonition as its own decision, remanded to Presbytery, and restored Bachmann to good standing, subject to possible pastoral oversight items 2–4.

title: Marusich v. Central Indiana Presbytery

title: Presbyterian Church in America v. Presbytery of the Mississippi Valley
synopsis: In a BCO 40-5 matter, the SJC held that a presbytery erred in upholding a session's erasure of a member who pled not guilty to failing to submit and pursued divorce. The session wrongly equated declining divorce counsel with refusing submission, failed to assess membership duties in another branch, failed to notify her of erasure, and proceeded without process after dropping charges. The SJC sustained the challenge, directed the session to note the notice failure and remove her under BCO 38-3(a), but ordered no express reversal.

title: Park et al. v. Korean Central Presbytery
synopsis: Teaching elders challenged Korean Central Presbytery’s summary censure of a minister before an indictment was prepared. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s action because discipline preceded particular charges and a specific confession, and because an independent church lacked authority to impose PCA censure. It declared the underlying matter moot because the alleged event was twenty-one years old and the victim would not cooperate, ending the proceeding without remand. The ruling addressed neither the allegations’ merits nor all old charges categorically.

title: Huffman v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery
synopsis: A filing challenging Presbytery’s handling of Huffman’s BCO 38-1 confession was styled as an appeal under a newly amended rule. The ruling found clear error, not an absence of all presbyterial review authority.

title: PCA v. Louisiana Presbytery (Trial)
synopsis: In this BCO 40-5 proceeding over Louisiana Presbytery’s investigation of TE Stephen Wilkins, the SJC dismissed Specification 1 because it could not find that the cited procedures were constitutionally required or that guilt was proved. Wilkins’s and his church’s withdrawal made practical amends unavailable.

title: Doty v. Nashville Presbytery

Presbytery properly treated the allegations as BCO 31-2/34-1 reports, and the complainant, not a Nashville member, lacked standing to complain about that new action. A nine-member dissent argued the filing of charges conferred standing under prior SJC cases.

title: Gendy v. Central Florida Presbytery

The SJC sustained the complaint: standing under BCO 43-1 cannot be defeated by the very removal challenged. Removal under BCO 38-4 is pastoral discipline, a disciplinary case, not a merely administrative act. The SJC remanded to Presbytery to consider the complaint and take the action it should have taken—remand to the Session. The merits of the removal were not decided.

title: Presbyterian Church in America v. Presbytery of the Mississippi Valley
synopsis: In a BCO 40-5 matter, the SJC held that a presbytery erred in upholding a session's erasure of a member who pled not guilty to failing to submit and pursued divorce. title: White v. Siouxlands Presbytery

The SJC denied the complaint. Applying BCO 39-3.3, it found no clear error in the lower courts’ credibility and discretionary judgments, given Session’s familiarity with the people and events. It characterized the restriction as informal pastoral safety guidance, not judicial discipline: it did not bar sacraments, worship elsewhere, or transfer, and attendance could resume upon medical assurance. The conditional local restriction therefore remained undisturbed.
